newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurd attack mars U.S. ceasefire in north Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Kurd attack mars U.S. ceasefire in north Iraq.

text.p: A Kurdish militia fired shells and Katyusha rockets at a rival faction in north Iraq on Thursday despite a U.S.-brokered truce to end two months of fighting that has damaged Washington's anti-Baghdad efforts.
Witnesses said the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) opened fire sporadically on Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) fighters at mid-morning near the town of Degala.

"There is no sign of a ceasefire," leading KDP commander Roj Nuri Shuwayis told Reuters. But his forces did not fire back and there were no immediate reports of clashes in other parts of the mountainous region.
A U.N. official in KDP-controlled Degala said the fighting made it impossible to organise a relief convoy to the PUK-held town of Koy Sanjak, about 30 km (19 miles) to the east.
"We can't go through because of the firing. We have enough food for the starving people of Koy Sanjak but we can't get through to help them," a senior U.N. official said in Degala.

U.S. envoy Robert Pelletreau got a ceasefire promise from the leaders of the two factions at separate meetings in Turkey this week and on Wednesday the U.S. State Department announced the groups had agreed to observe a ceasefire from midnight Iraqi time (2000 GMT on Wednesday).
The PUK of Jalal Talabani said earlier that it had told its forces to stop fighting.

"There were orders to that effect on the ground yesterday because we were expecting (the ceasefire), but we haven't been in contact with Iraqi Kurdistan this morning," said Shazad Saib, the PUK's Turkey's representative.
Iraqi newspapers have urged the Kurds to abandon the U.S. effort and instead come to Baghdad for peace talks.

"The warring Kurdish parties should leave aside playing with the vicious foreign card and start national dialogue (in Baghdad) to end their bloody fighting," said al-Thawra newspaper, organ of the ruling Baath party.

This latgest bout of fighting erupted at the end of August when the KDP called on Baghdad's forces for help in taking control of the main regional city of Arbil, which had been in PUK hands since late 1994.

The Iraqi move prompted retaliatory U.S. missile strikes against Iraqi military targets and since then the United States, which leads an air operation to protect north Iraq from Baghdad's troops, has warned Iraq against further involvement.
The United States has since evacuated most of its employees in the north, as well as the military command centre of the air force in place since Baghdad's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War.
Massoud Barzani's KDP, which had threatened to call on Iraq again for help, accuses Iran of backing Talabani's PUK. Both Tehran and the PUK deny the charges.

Many ceasefires between the two groups have been called and broken since fighting first flared up in late 1994. But a diplomat in Ankara involved in the latest peace bid said he was confident the factions would lay down their arms.
"It will take a little time for the orders to filter through," he said. "It has reached a stalemate," he said.
Delegations from the warring parties are to meet in the Turkish capital next week to move the peace process forward.
